lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- Castings for a New Kind of Car
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Julius Cesar do Nascimento | Lesson 2 -- Castings for a New Kind of Car
lesson.grammar_point: passive voice in different tenses: is made, was designed, has been replaced, is being tested, will be needed (be in the right tense + past participle)

listenings.text: I work as a process engineer at an aluminum foundry in Michigan, and people always ask me how a casting is made. So here's the short version. First, the metal is melted in a furnace at about seven hundred degrees Celsius. Then the molten aluminum is poured into the machine, and it's pushed into a steel mold under very high pressure. The whole thing takes less than two minutes. When the part comes out, it's cooled, it's checked by a camera, and the extra metal around the edges is cut off. Nothing is wasted. That extra metal is collected as scrap and melted again the same day. Finally, the parts are machined, and they're sent to the customer. Last year, more than a million parts were made on this line.

Our company has been building casting machines in the north of Italy for more than fifty years. Most of them are sold to car makers and to their suppliers. A few years ago, we were asked to build something very big: a machine that could cast a large part of a car in one piece. At first, many people said it was impossible. Today, machines like this are used in factories in the United States, in China and in Europe. But I always tell my customers the truth. A giant machine is not a magic solution. The molds are very expensive, and they have to be changed regularly. And if the design of the car is changed, a new mold has to be made. So my advice is simple. Start with one part, learn, and then decide.

I buy parts for a car maker in France, and my job has changed a lot in the last three years. Before, most of the parts that I bought were made of steel or cast iron, and many of them were made for engines. Now we're building more electric cars, so fewer engine parts are needed. What do we need instead? Lightweight components, made of aluminum, that are delivered ready to install. That means the parts have to be cast, machined and checked by the same supplier. A supplier who only casts is not enough for us anymore. And there's one more question that is always asked in our meetings now. How much of your aluminum is recycled? Our customers want to know, so we want to know too.

paras: For about a hundred years, the body of a car has been built in the same way. Many small pieces of steel are pressed into shape, and then they are welded together by robots. A typical rear floor, for example, was made of seventy or more components. In the last few years, a different idea has been tested by some electric car makers: the same section is cast in one single piece of aluminum alloy. Molten metal is poured into a giant mold under very high pressure, and about two minutes later a large casting comes out.

The advantages are easy to see. Fewer parts are needed, many welding robots are replaced by one machine, and the car becomes more lightweight, which is important when a heavy battery is carried under the floor. But there are problems too. A giant casting is expensive to repair after an accident, and if a mold is damaged, a whole production line can stop. The process is still being improved, and many engineers believe that it will be used for some parts of the car, not for all of them.

What does this mean for a traditional foundry? Cast iron is still used for engine blocks, brake discs and heavy machinery, and it will be needed for many years. But as cars become electric, fewer engine parts will be ordered. Foundries that have supplied the car industry for decades are now being asked a hard question by their customers: can you cast aluminum, and can you machine it in the same plant? Scrap is another opportunity. Most aluminum can be melted and cast again and again, and buyers are starting to ask how much of it is recycled.
